summary: How blockchain works — blocks, hashes, chains, distributed ledgers and consensus — and where blockchain technology is used.

blocks.content: A **decentralised, distributed digital ledger** in which records (transactions) are grouped into **blocks** that are **linked in a chain by cryptographic hashes** and copied to many computers (**nodes**), so that records cannot be changed without detection.

items.title: Block
items.content: Contains a set of **transactions/data**, a **timestamp**, its own **hash**, and the **hash of the previous block**.

items.title: Hash
items.content: A fixed-length "fingerprint" calculated from the block's contents (e.g. SHA-256). Changing even one character gives a completely different hash.

items.title: Chain
items.content: Each block stores the previous block's hash, so blocks are linked in order back to the first (**genesis**) block.

items.title: Distributed ledger
items.content: Every node keeps a **full copy** of the blockchain; there is no central authority.

items.title: Consensus
items.content: Nodes must **agree** before a new block is added — e.g. **proof of work** (mining: solving a hard puzzle) or **proof of stake**.

blocks.title: Adding a transaction
items: A user requests a transaction (e.g. send 1 coin to Asel), signed with their **private key**.
The transaction is **broadcast** to the network of nodes.
Valid transactions are grouped into a new **block**.
Nodes reach **consensus** (e.g. a miner solves the proof-of-work puzzle).
The block is **added to the chain** on every node; the transaction is complete.

blocks.title: Why it is tamper-resistant
blocks.content: If someone changes data in Block 2, its hash changes, so Block 3's "previous hash" no longer matches and the chain is broken. The attacker would have to recalculate every following block **on most of the nodes at once**, which is practically impossible.

blocks.title: Uses of blockchain
rows: Programs on the blockchain that run automatically when conditions are met
Tracking food or medicines from producer to shop

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
rows: Very hard to tamper with — high data integrity
Proof of work uses huge amounts of **electricity**
No central authority or single point of failure
Slow and limited number of transactions per second
Mistakes cannot be undone; lost private keys = lost assets
Lower cost for some transactions (no intermediaries)
Legal and regulatory uncertainty; used in some crimes
Data stored on a public chain is visible (privacy)
